questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A survey that reported almost nothing
questions.learningObjective: assess a regional survey that found little
questions.stem: A regional survey reports that a district contains very few sites, having walked a large area systematically and recorded almost nothing. A later, larger project in the same district finds thousands of sites, many of them in ground the first survey had covered. Which statement about the two results is soundest?

options.text: The two are incompatible, since a district either contains sites or it does not and both projects looked at the same ground
options.misconception: assumes a survey measures the ground rather than a method of looking

options.text: The first survey is the better evidence, since it covered more ground and a larger sample is always better
options.misconception: prefers extent over intensity without argument

options.text: The two are compatible, since a survey's density depends on how much time it spends at each spot, and a rapid covering of a large area can miss most of what a slow survey of a small area finds
The later project's count proves the first survey was careless, since a professional survey does not miss sites
options.misconception: concludes carelessness from a disagreement about results

questions.explanation: This is the standard shape of a survey controversy, and the resolution is almost always about sampling effort rather than about the ground. A systematic surface survey that walks a district at a certain density and spends a fixed time at each stop is measuring the density of what is visible at the surface at that density; anything buried, anything under a crop, anything without a surface expression, and anything outside the corridor walked is outside its reach. A project that commits ten times the effort per hectare, adds remote sensing and test excavation, and returns a figure in the thousands is not correcting an error in the first count, it is measuring a different thing. What makes the second result damaging to the first is the overlap of ground: if the same places were walked and yielded nothing, the explanation has to lie in what was looked for and how long it was looked for, and that is a fair and answerable question.
questions.hint: Ask how much time the first survey spent at each spot, and what it was in a position to see.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order in which a chronology is rescued
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a floating sequence is anchored
questions.stem: A long ring series has been measured from a site and is internally consistent, but no year in it can yet be named. The steps by which it is put on the calendar are set out below. Place them in the order in which they must happen.

options.text: Samples of the wood are taken and dated, so the series has a physical age that can be compared with the ring measurements
The series is compared ring for ring against dated series from a wider area, and a long coincidence is found that fixes the whole series to particular years
The dated series that provided the match is extended backwards in time, and the overlap is tested again to see whether the two still agree
The date implied for buildings and deposits in the excavated deposits is read off the series, so the site's chronology becomes expressible in calendar years

questions.explanation: The order is one of supply before demand: the series has to be attached to something dated before it can be dated, and the something has to be tested before it is trusted. Sampling and dating come first because the match needs a physical age to compare, not merely a pattern to compare, since two patterns can coincide by chance and a pattern plus an age cannot. The ring-for-ring comparison comes second, and a long coincidence is what converts a relative sequence into an absolute one. Extending the dated series backwards comes third, and this is the step that decides whether the whole procedure is sound, since a floating sequence can be matched to a dated series by chance and only a sustained agreement over a long overlap gives reason to think the match is real. Reading dates off for the buildings comes last, and everything the site says about itself depends on it having been done in that order.
questions.hint: Ask what the match needs before it can be made, and what tests whether the match is real.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A drought and the year it is dated to
questions.learningObjective: assess a proxy that links a climate signal to a dated event
questions.stem: A study reports that a cave deposit and a set of lake sediments both indicate a period of reduced rainfall across a wide region, and that the same period contains the destruction layer of several settlements. The study concludes that drought caused the destructions. Which statement about that conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The two sets of evidence show that a drought and the destructions occurred together, and showing that they occurred together is the first of several steps rather than the last
The conclusion follows directly, since a drought reduces a harvest and a failed harvest precedes a destruction
options.misconception: assumes that a drought leads to a destruction without a step

options.text: The conclusion is unsound, since a cave deposit cannot show the rainfall of a region, only the conditions inside the cave
options.misconception: objecting to the scale at which a proxy can be read

options.text: The conclusion is unsound, since settlements are destroyed by people and a climate cannot act on a person
options.misconception: denies that a climate can act on a decision

questions.explanation: Coincidence in time is a necessary part of most causal arguments and nowhere near a sufficient one, and the gap between them is where the work of such a study is done. Having established that a drought and the destructions belong to the same period, the questions still open include whether the drought was severe enough over the right months in the right places, whether the destructions were of settlements that depended on the harvest that failed, and what the settlements did about it. Those are not pedantic questions, since a society that had stored grain, or had access to a market, or had a political structure that could move people, would be affected by a drought quite differently from one that had none of those. The study as described has established a coincidence well, which is a real contribution, and the difference between its conclusion and what the coincidence licenses is the difference between a hypothesis and a demonstration.
questions.hint: Ask what has been shown about the timing, and what would have to be added to turn that into a cause.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collapse that began before the drought
questions.learningObjective: use a chronology to reorder a cause and its putative effect
questions.stem: A region of lowland cities declines over a period of about two centuries, and a study finds that the political disruption in the southern part of the region begins earlier than in the north, while the droughts that the study identifies as the stress are both more severe in the south and later in the sequence. Which inference does the ordering support?

options.text: In the south the drought must have been the first thing that went wrong, since the earlier political disruption was itself caused by the drought that came later
options.misconception: infers backwards causation from a sequence

options.text: In the south the drought cannot be the first thing that went wrong, so a prior stress has to be sought, and the drought is at most an aggravator
The ordering proves the drought did nothing at all, since a cause cannot act on a society that has already begun to decline
options.misconception: treats an aggravator as having no effect

options.text: The ordering shows the study's chronology is wrong, since a drought cannot be later than a political change in the same region
options.misconception: rejects a chronology for a relationship between two variables

questions.explanation: A chronology is an argument, and this one does real work because it excludes a candidate rather than merely supporting one. If the political disruption in the south begins before the severe droughts, then whatever caused the disruption cannot be the drought, and an explanation that had made the drought the initiating cause has to be modified. The modified version is the more interesting one, since a society already under political strain is a society in which a drought is more likely to produce abandonment than in an intact one, so the drought becomes an accelerant whose effect depends on the condition of the thing it acts upon. What the ordering does not do is identify the prior stress, and a study that stops at the exclusion has not explained the south. That is worth saying because an exclusion is frequently reported as though it were a finding, and the discipline of the two apart is one of the more useful things a chronology can teach.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two came first in the place where the two do not agree.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A region that did not decline
questions.learningObjective: weigh evidence that complicates a story of general decline
questions.stem: A widely taught account holds that the city-states of a lowland region declined and were abandoned between the eighth and tenth centuries. A survey of the region finds that abandonment was not general: some centres in the same region continued to be occupied, one centre to the north grew for a century after the southern centres had declined, and one southern centre shows a period of substantial building after the beginning of the general decline. Which of the following follow from that survey? Select all that apply.

options.text: The account of a general decline describes a majority of sites rather than all of them, and should be restated with that limit
The later growth at one centre shows that the region's economy was still capable of supporting large building projects at that later date
The growth at one northern centre shows that the climate was not deteriorating across the region during the period
options.misconception: reads a regional climate claim out of one centre's growth

options.text: The continued occupation of some centres shows that the cause of the decline must have been a natural event, since a natural event would not spare them
options.misconception: infers a cause from the pattern of who was spared

options.text: The later building at one southern centre shows that the decline was a single event rather than a process
options.misconception: infers a single event from the fact that one place recovered

questions.explanation: The two defensible statements are the two that restate the claim without exceeding it. A majority is not a totality, and a general claim about a region that turns out to hold for some sites and not others is not thereby false; it is imprecise, and the fix is a word. The growth of a large centre after the southern decline has begun is evidence about capacity, since a society that can still put up monumental buildings can still command labour and materials, and that is a fact about the region's economy at a date when the general account would have it in terminal decline. The three indefensible statements each over-read the pattern. Growth at one place says nothing definitive about a region's climate, who was spared says nothing about the cause, and one centre that recovered is evidence for a process that can go differently depending on the place, not evidence for a single moment.
questions.hint: Ask which of the survey's findings state a limit on the account, and which of them explain it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The thing a carbon test dates
questions.learningObjective: state what a radiocarbon result is a date of
questions.stem: A laboratory is sent a sample of charred grain from a storage pit and returns a measurement expressed in years before a fixed reference year, along with an uncertainty of some tens of years. The report also says the calibration curve has been applied and that the result corresponds to a range of calendar years rather than a single one. Which statement about that report is correct?

options.text: The measurement is a date of the carbon in the grain, so it is a date of the growth of the crop, and a pit can be dug, filled and sealed well after the crop was grown
The measurement is a date of the pit, so the result bounds when the pit was dug and no other date can be read from it
options.misconception: treats a date of material as a date of the context that holds it

options.text: The measurement is a date of the laboratory's work, since the grain is destroyed by the test and its age is known only from what the instrument recorded
options.misconception: mistakes the act of measurement for the thing measured

options.text: The measurement is a date of the calendar, so the range in the report is a statement of the lab's uncertainty about which year system is in use
options.misconception: reinterprets a calibrated range as a disagreement about calendars

questions.explanation: The single most useful habit in this subject is to keep asking what the material was and what happened to it, because a carbon test says something narrow and a great deal has to be done to widen it. What the test can say is when the carbon in the sample stopped exchanging with the atmosphere, and for a grain that is the year it grew. Everything after that is stratigraphy: the grain was harvested, stored, and put in a pit, and the pit was filled, and the pit was sealed, and the pit was buried under something else, and each of those steps is a separate event with a separate date and a separate uncertainty, and the only one the measurement bears on is the first. This is why a carbon date is reported as a range rather than a year, why the same material can be dated in two laboratories and give two results, and why a well-built site still has to be excavated to find out which of its events the sample belongs to.
questions.hint: Ask when the material stopped exchanging with the air, and how many events happened after that.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A constant remeasured and a table of dates that moves
questions.learningObjective: explain the consequence of changing a constant used to compute a published series
questions.stem: For decades, ages in the carbon dating literature were computed using a half-life of 5,568 years, which is the value the method's founders had measured, together with a fixed reference year of 1950. A later and better measurement gave 5,730 years, and the convention of computing published ages with the original 5,568 was kept so that the figures in the older literature would remain comparable. A table of 200 published ages is therefore expressed in units computed from a half-life now known to be about three per cent short. Which statement about the table is best supported?

options.text: Every age in the table is wrong by the same three per cent, so a reader can simply multiply the whole column by 1.03 and recover the calendar years
options.misconception: assumes a single global scaling factor converts a convention into a calendar age

options.text: The table is unusable, since a table computed from a constant known to be wrong cannot support any inference at all
options.misconception: condemns a series for a defect every reader can state

options.text: Every age in the table is a consistent number in a stated convention, and each corresponds to a different interval of calendar time, so the table is internally usable and cannot be read as calendar years without a further step
The table is unaffected, since the reference year rather than the half-life determines the age a sample is assigned
options.misconception: identifies the wrong parameter as the one that matters

questions.explanation: A convention is a rule that everybody follows, and the value of following one is that numbers from different laboratories and different decades can be compared at all, which is exactly what the 1950 reference year buys and what the original half-life buys. The cost is that the numbers are not calendar years, and the cost is not uniform: the relationship between a computed age and a calendar interval depends on how much the atmosphere's carbon has varied over the interval in question, so a date near the reference year is barely affected while a date several thousand years away moves by a different amount from its neighbour. That is why the correction is applied through a calibration curve rather than by a single multiplier, and why the item's fourth option fails on inspection: the reference year fixes where zero is, and the half-life fixes the shape of the curve, and a series needs both.
questions.hint: Ask what the convention buys, and what it costs, in terms of comparing dates and reading them as years.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two half-lives and two answers
questions.learningObjective: compute the shift a remeasured half-life produces in a published age
questions.stem: A sample is reported as 11,136 years before the reference year, a figure computed by counting two half-lives of 5,568 years from the reference date. A student recomputes the same measurement using the later half-life of 5,730 years, assuming the proportion of carbon remaining is unchanged and the atmosphere's carbon is constant over the interval. By how many years does the student answer differ from the published figure?

options.text: The student obtains 11,136 years, which is unchanged, because a half-life fixes a proportion rather than a length of time
options.misconception: confuses the two definitions of a half-life

options.text: The student obtains 11,460 years, which is 324 years older, because two of the longer half-lives contain 324 more years
The student obtains 10,812 years, which is 324 years younger, because a longer half-life means the sample took longer to decay
options.misconception: inverts the direction in which a longer half-life moves the answer

options.text: The student obtains 5,730 years, which is half as long again, because only one of the two half-lives needs to be recomputed
options.misconception: halves the interval without a stated reason

questions.explanation: A half-life is a length of time in which half of a sample decays, so two half-lives leave a quarter of the original, and a sample reported at 11,136 years is at two half-lives of 5,568. Recomputing with 5,730 gives 2 x 5,730 = 11,460, and the difference is 11,460 - 11,136 = 324 years. The sign is worth being careful about, because it is the direction the two conventions pull in opposite ways: with the longer half-life, a given fraction of carbon remaining is reached later, so the same measurement yields a larger number of years. The third option is the trap, and it reverses that, treating a longer half-life as a faster decay. The fourth shows the other common error, forgetting that a reported age may represent more than one half-life, which is precisely what the stated figure of 11,136 depends on.
questions.hint: Ask what fraction of the carbon remains after two half-lives, and recompute the interval with the longer half-life.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A beam older than the room that stands on it
questions.learningObjective: explain the effect of reusing old timber on a date
questions.stem: A building is dated by a sample taken from the centre of one of its main beams, and the measured age of the carbon comes out some centuries earlier than the building's foundation date established from bricks and documents. A second sample is taken from the outer rings of a beam in the same building and returns a date close to the foundation date. Which feature of the first sample best explains the discrepancy?

options.text: The sample was contaminated by the mortar in the wall, since carbon in lime and carbon in wood are measured the same way
options.misconception: invents a contamination route the two samples would share

options.text: The beam was reused from an earlier building, so the discrepancy shows that the wood was old before the room was built
options.misconception: supplies a second mechanism where the first is sufficient

options.text: The measurement was too imprecise to distinguish the two dates, since an uncertainty of some decades cannot be resolved against a difference of centuries
options.misconception: claims a precision problem where the two samples agree

options.text: The sample came from the middle of a tree, and a tree's inner rings formed decades or centuries before the tree was felled, so the measurement dates the growth of the wood rather than the building

questions.explanation: The difference between the heart of a tree and its outer rings is the whole of this item, and it is one of the commonest sources of a date that is confidently wrong. A tree adds a ring to the outside every year while it lives, so the material at the centre of a trunk began forming when the tree was a sapling, and the material at the outside formed in the year it was felled. A sample from the middle therefore dates a growth episode that ended long before the tree was cut, and that gap between the date of the growth and the date of the felling is the tree's own age, which for an oak used in a building can be a century or more. That is why the second sample, taken from the outer rings, agrees with the bricks, and why a specification for a timber sample normally asks for the outer rings or a sequence of rings from the bark inwards.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the tree the sample came from, and when that part formed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A shell that grew in the sea
questions.learningObjective: explain why a marine sample returns an age that is not the age of the shell
questions.stem: A sample of shell from a midden on a coast is dated, and the returned age is earlier than the midden's known date of filling by several centuries. A lake deposit in the same region returns ages that are anomalously old by hundreds of years, and the laboratory warns that samples from both kinds of site need particular care. Which feature common to the two cases explains the direction of the error?

options.text: The carbon in both is partly drawn from material that was already old when the organism grew, so the measured proportion of carbon is lower than it should be and the age comes out greater
The carbon in both is diluted by carbon from the air, so the measured proportion is higher and the age comes out smaller
options.misconception: inverts both the direction and the size of the effect

options.text: Both are harder than land samples to clean, so the uncertainty in both is large and the direction of the difference is an artefact of cleaning
options.misconception: makes the error a laboratory failure rather than a property of the material

options.text: Both are younger than they appear, so the disagreement with the known dates shows the midden and the deposit are both misdated
options.misconception: reverses the direction stated in the passage

questions.explanation: The effect has a name and a mechanism, and the name is the reservoir effect, which is worth learning as a mechanism rather than a label. Seawater carries dissolved carbon that includes carbon from limestone, from the shells of organisms that died long ago, and from water that has been in contact with rock; an organism that builds its shell in that water incorporates carbon from that reservoir and not only from the air it breathes. Freshwater has its own version, since water passing through limestone picks up 'old' carbon from the rock and gives it to plants and then to everything that eats them. In both cases the sample therefore contains some carbon that had already stopped exchanging with the atmosphere, and the effect of that is to make the sample look older than it is, in a direction that is known and quantifiable. The laboratory's warning is the practical consequence: samples like these can be dated, but only with a stated adjustment and a stated uncertainty.
questions.hint: Ask where the carbon in the sample came from, and what happens to the measurement if part of it was already old.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A burial that was doing something else
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the practice a context represents from its ostensible purpose
questions.stem: At a site, a deposit of ash, broken pots and animal bone lies inside a pit whose shape matches a burial cut, and a body is not present. A study argues that the deposit was placed deliberately and that the pit was made to be seen, rather than that a burial was disturbed. Which feature of the deposit is most consistent with the study's reading?

options.text: The absence of a body proves that the burial was disturbed, since a pit of that shape cannot have been made for anything else
options.misconception: treats one absence as a demonstration rather than as a puzzle

options.text: The deposit lies inside a pit, so its location establishes that it is a burial whatever its contents happen to be
options.misconception: lets the container decide the question the contents raise

options.text: The deposit's contents are placed in a deliberate order and include material with no ordinary use at a funeral, so the assemblage is being put on show rather than consumed
The deposit contains animal bone, so it belongs with the other burials in the same cemetery period and needs no separate explanation
options.misconception: explains a deposit by its date and location rather than by its contents

questions.explanation: An archaeologist reads a deposit as a set of relationships rather than as a label, and the two habits produce different accounts of the same pit. A burial is not identified by the shape of the hole but by the combination of a body, a container, an orientation, a set of objects, and a position in relation to others, and a pit with a careful arrangement of objects and no body is a different kind of deposit. The study's reading has an ordinary motive behind it: a deposit whose contents could not be used up, arranged where it could be seen, is doing something that a funeral deposit does not do, and the most economical explanation is that the point of it was the display. The competing explanations in the distractors all rest on a single feature, and the fourth is the one to be most careful about, since a shared date and a shared place are exactly the conditions under which deposits with different purposes are most often merged into a single story.
questions.hint: Ask what the deposit is made of and how it is arranged, before asking where it was put.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A tree ring that has to be matched first
questions.learningObjective: explain how a relative sequence becomes an absolute chronology
questions.stem: A tree from a site gives a long series of rings whose widths are measured. The series contains a pattern distinctive enough to be recognised, and the pattern reappears, ring for ring, in a series from a tree whose outermost ring is known to have grown in a year a document records. Which step in the procedure is being described?

options.text: Counting the rings from the outside inwards, which gives the age of the tree directly without any need for a second series
options.misconception: claims a direct age where a match is what supplies the anchor

options.text: Matching the distinctive pattern to the dated series, which anchors the undated one and converts a sequence of relative widths into years
Measuring the width of the widest ring, since the widest ring in a series is always the one a known year produced
options.misconception: supposes a single ring identifies a year

options.text: Comparing the total number of rings with a published figure for the region, since a region's trees are assumed to be the same age
options.misconception: assumes every tree in a region grew for the same number of years

questions.explanation: This is the single idea on which the whole of the method depends, and it is worth stating plainly because it is counter-intuitive. A measured ring width series carries no dates at all: it is a pattern of narrow and wide years, and on its own it can only tell you the order of those years, not which year any of them was. The anchoring comes from overlap. Somewhere else there is a series whose dates are already known, usually because it runs to the present day through living and recently dead trees, and where a long enough run of the two series coincides ring for ring, the whole of the undated series is fixed to the calendar. That is why the method is called cross-dating, why a match has to be long enough to be improbable, and why a floating sequence, one that cannot be matched to anything dated, is genuinely undated rather than approximately dated, and why the effort to find an overlap for a floating sequence is one of the most consequential single pieces of work in the subject.
questions.hint: Ask what the undated series contains on its own, and what the other series supplies.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A tree that lost a ring
questions.learningObjective: explain the consequence of a missing ring for a match
questions.stem: In a bad year a tree may put down no visible ring, and a matching exercise between two series then finds that the sequences agree except at one point, where the dated series has a ring the undated series does not. Which move does a careful worker make?

options.text: Reject the match, since a single disagreement in a long series shows the two sequences are of different trees and of different ages
options.misconception: makes one disagreement decisive in a series built on long overlap

options.text: Add a ring to the undated series at the point of disagreement, since the width of a missing ring can be estimated from its neighbours
options.misconception: supplies a measurement the case gives no basis for

options.text: Shorten both series by a year at the point of disagreement, so that the remainder of the overlap lines up and the anchor is preserved
options.misconception: patches the disagreement by discarding data

options.text: Treat the disagreement as a possible missing ring rather than a misdate, and check whether the rest of the overlap is exact, since a genuine match is not thereby destroyed

questions.explanation: A tree ring chronology is a physical record of physiology, and physiology does not always oblige, so a ring can be absent for a whole season in a tree that was not dead. That possibility has to be built into the method, and it is, because the diagnostic feature of a genuine match is a long run of exact correspondence rather than a perfect one, and because the distribution of false matches falls off sharply with the length of the overlap. The practical consequence is that a worker confronted with a single disagreement inside an otherwise exact long overlap will look for the ecological reason for the missing ring, since a drought or a fire or an insect attack is usually recorded in the growth of other trees from the same year as well. The fourth option is the failure mode to avoid, since adjusting the series to save the match is precisely the operation that turns a dating method into a way of confirming whatever the anchor happened to be.
questions.hint: Ask whether one disagreement in a long exact overlap is a reason to abandon the match.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The air trapped in an ice core
questions.learningObjective: explain why gas and ice in a core carry different dates
questions.stem: A core of ice from a polar sheet contains, between the ice layers, bubbles of air that were sealed off when the snow that became the ice was compressed. A study reports that the gas in a bubble is younger than the ice immediately above it. Which feature of the core accounts for that difference?

options.text: The gas has leaked upward through the firn, so the bubbles nearest the surface hold the oldest air in the core
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which the age increases

options.text: Air is enclosed at a depth above the ice in which it is finally found, and the younger gas has therefore travelled further down with the ice than the ice that sealed it
The ice is dated by the ash in it and the gas by the dust, and the two differ because ash falls seasonally and dust is transported
options.misconception: invents two unrelated dating signals to explain one difference

options.text: The difference is an instrument artefact, since a core cannot hold both solid and gaseous material in sequence
options.misconception: denies a well-established property of ice cores

questions.explanation: The age difference between ice and the air it holds is a small correction with large consequences, and it arises because the two are closed at different moments. Snow accumulates as a porous firn, and the pore spaces stay connected to the atmosphere until compaction has closed them, so an air bubble is sealed at some depth rather than at the surface; the ice around it, meanwhile, continues to compact and flow downwards for a long time after the bubble formed. The result is a gas that is younger than the ice above it, by an interval that grows with depth and with the rate of flow, and that has to be subtracted or added consistently before any two samples can be compared. This is why an ice core is described as carrying two chronologies rather than one, and why the correction is a condition of using a core to align one gas layer with an ice layer somewhere else.
questions.hint: Ask at what moment the air is sealed, compared with the moment the ice above it formed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An ash layer that ties four sites together
questions.learningObjective: explain what a shared tephra layer does for a chronology
questions.stem: A fall of ash is identified in the deposits of four settlements across a region, and the glass shards in all four are shown to have the same chemical composition. None of the four settlements is dated independently. Which conclusion follows from the evidence?

options.text: The four deposits were laid down at the same time, so the four sites can be placed in a common sequence that the ash fixes, even though no individual site has been dated
The four sites are of the same age, since a shared layer means the settlements themselves were founded together
options.misconception: infers a date of foundation from a date of deposition

options.text: The four sites are in sequence, since an ash layer settles progressively as a site is abandoned
options.misconception: supposes a depositional order that settling ash does not have

options.text: Nothing follows, since a chemical match shows only that the four deposits share a source and says nothing about when they were laid down
options.misconception: insists a source match carries no chronological information

questions.explanation: The value of a tephra layer is that it is an isochron: a single depositional event whose material can be recognised wherever it fell, which makes it the closest thing archaeology has to a fixed point. The chemical comparison is what makes the recognition reliable, since two eruptions can produce superficially similar ash and a compositional fingerprint distinguishes them. Once the layer is matched across four sites, two things follow at once, and both are large. The four deposits share a date, which is often the only way to relate sites that have no artefacts or structures in common; and the layer's position within each site's sequence ties that site's earlier and later deposits to the other three, so a single radiocarbon date anywhere in the group constrains all of them. What does not follow is anything about the foundations of the settlements, since a deposit is a later event that has nothing to say about when the place was first occupied.
questions.hint: Ask whether the layer dates the deposit or the settlement, and what a chemical match establishes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The last firing of a pot
questions.learningObjective: explain what a heat-dating method measures
questions.stem: A method applied to a fired clay vessel measures an energy that had been stored in the clay by radiation and that is released when the object is heated in a laboratory furnace; the energy released, and the way it is released, indicate the temperature the object was last taken to. Which statement about what the method dates is correct?

options.text: It dates the first time the object was fired, since the earliest heating is the one that altered the clay permanently
options.misconception: supplies a first firing where the method reads the last

options.text: It dates the burial of the object, since the clock starts when the object enters the ground
options.misconception: puts the start of the clock at an event that does not reset it

options.text: It dates the manufacture of the clay, since the properties measured belong to the material rather than to the firing
options.misconception: confuses a property of the material with a property of the event

options.text: It dates the last time the object was fired, since the stored energy is emptied by a heating and accumulates again only through another firing

questions.explanation: The logic of the method is a clock that is emptied and then recharged, and once that structure is clear the rest follows. The energy the method releases was put into the crystal structure of the clay by radiation while the object sat in the ground, and every heating above a threshold drives it out; a pot that has been fired, buried, heated in a laboratory, and left is a pot whose stored energy was emptied by the laboratory, which is why a laboratory firing is destructive and why an object that has been reheated since it was made will return a date for the reheating rather than for the maker. The useful consequence is the one the item is really about: the method dates an event, and events can happen twice, so a date is a statement about the object's history and not about the moment somebody shaped it, and a sherd that has been through a kiln twice will date to the second firing.
questions.hint: Ask what empties the stored energy, and what has to happen afterwards for it to build up again.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An eponym who outlived his reign
questions.learningObjective: explain the dating consequence of naming a year after a ruler
questions.stem: A list of events is dated by naming the ruler or the administrator in office, and a single such name appears for events that a text shows to lie on both sides of that person's death. Which feature of eponymous dating is best illustrated by that?

options.text: The events cannot both be true, since one ruler cannot be in office at two separated times
options.misconception: supposes an office can be held only once

options.text: The name must refer to a different person in the later events, which is the ordinary way such lists are resolved
options.misconception: assumes a single solution where a mistranscription is equally possible

options.text: The name is a label applied by a later compiler rather than a fixed point in the sequence, so events assigned to it can fall before, during or after the office it names
The name dates nothing at all, since a list of this kind is decorative and carries no chronological information
options.misconception: dismisses a device that exists precisely to carry dates

questions.explanation: Naming an event after the official in office is one of the oldest and one of the most troublesome devices in the subject, and its difficulty is structural rather than accidental. The device is an association between an event and a person, and the association is made by somebody writing later, from a list, with an interest in making the list usable. Nothing in the device guarantees that the compiler knew which of several people sharing a name he meant, or that he placed an event in the right year, and the commonest form of the error is a name being carried forward, so that events before the office, during it, and after it all acquire the same label. The result is a chronological framework whose only hard points are the beginning and the end of the named office, which is why historians using such a list spend so much of their effort on the fixed points at its edges and treat the interior as needing corroboration from something dated by another method altogether.
questions.hint: Ask whether the name is a fixed point in the sequence or a label applied to a group of events.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two chronologies a century apart
questions.learningObjective: explain how a dated synchronism and a dated sample can disagree
questions.stem: For the great eruption that buried a Bronze Age town, radiocarbon measurements on short-lived material sealed by the ash give dates around 1600 BC, while synchronisms with events recorded in the texts of a neighbouring kingdom place it about a century later, near 1500 BC. A review of the debate concludes that the discrepancy is at least in part a modern artefact of how the evidence has been assembled. Which statement about the two chronologies is soundest?

options.text: The two are independent measurements, so the mean of the two estimates is the best available date for the eruption
options.misconception: averages a physical measurement with a chain of historical inference

options.text: The two are not independent measurements of the same thing, since the texts fix the date only through a chain of synchronisms, and the error in any link of that chain is transferred to the eruption
The radiocarbon dates are the better evidence and the synchronisms are superseded, since a laboratory measurement of the ash is a direct observation of the event
options.misconception: confuses a direct measurement of material with a direct measurement of the event

options.text: The discrepancy shows that one of the two bodies of evidence has been falsified, since two chronologies cannot both stand
options.misconception: makes a discrepancy into a demonstration of fraud

questions.explanation: The two chronologies are attached to different things, and the difference is not a disagreement about the same measurement. A radiocarbon date on material sealed by the ash is a measurement of the carbon, converted to a calendar range by a curve, and its weakness is a known and quantifiable one. A synchronism is an inference that the eruption and an event mentioned in somebody's text happened at the same time, and each such step in that chain carries its own uncertainty, which the final date inherits. Two chronologies built this way can differ by a century without either being wrong, and the practical consequence is that a whole region's dating shifts with the resolution of the dispute, which is why the dispute matters far beyond the eruption itself. The third option names the confusion to avoid: measuring the carbon directly is not measuring the eruption directly, since the sample and the event are separated by the burial, and the material could be a generation old.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two dates is a date of, and how many steps each one involves.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The specimen that looked perfect and was set aside
questions.learningObjective: assess a dating argument that rests on an assumption about the material
questions.stem: A charred branch found sealed in the ash of a Bronze Age eruption was for years the key date for the eruption, on the reasoning that a tree's annual rings can be matched against a dated ring sequence, which is the most precise kind of dating available. Later work questioned whether olive trees lay down rings reliably enough in that climate for the match to be made at all, and a further specimen from a neighbouring island was dated instead. Which statement about the first specimen is best supported?

options.text: The reasoning was sound in form and rested on an untested assumption about how the tree grew, so the specimen was never disqualified by its own dates but by a fact about the material that the method needed and had not checked
The reasoning was circular, since a tree that grew near the eruption cannot also be used to date it
options.misconception: calls a method circular that is standard practice

options.text: The specimen should be discarded, since a doubt about one tree's rings discredits every ring series ever built from that species
options.misconception: extends a doubt about a specimen to a whole method

options.text: The specimen remains the best date, since a competing specimen from another island cannot be compared with one from the island itself
options.misconception: assumes a sample from another island is incomparable without a stated reason

questions.explanation: Every dating method has a precondition, and the interesting failures are the ones where the precondition is assumed rather than tested. Ring matching requires that the tree lay down one ring per year and that the rings be wide enough to measure and distinctive enough to match; for most species in most places that is safe to assume, and for a species in an unusual climate it is not. The first specimen was not refuted by any of its own numbers, which is what makes the case instructive, and it was not refuted by a rival specimen either, since a second specimen is a second attempt rather than a contradiction. The failure was at the level of the method's premise, and the discipline it calls for is to ask, of any spectacular date that depends on a technique's working well, what had to be true about the material for the technique to work, and whether anybody has checked it.
questions.hint: Ask what the technique needed from the tree, and whether that was tested before the date was built on it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An anomaly reassigned to a different volcano
questions.learningObjective: follow a correction made by a chemical fingerprint

stimulus.body: From a report on the alignment of tree rings and polar ice cores: 'A growth anomaly in northern tree rings had been identified with a large eruption in the seventeenth century BC and used for decades as the fixed point that tied those rings to the ice. We re-examine the alignment and compare the glass chemistry of the ice-core deposit with reference samples. The deposit matches a known eruption in Alaska, and does not match the volcano to which it had been assigned. The date remains the same; the volcano changes. On the corrected alignment, the eruption in question is not among the candidates that remain, and three later deposits become the remaining possibilities for the island eruption.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the report. Which statement about the correction is best supported?

options.text: The date is now known to be wrong, since a date and a volcano are a single fact and the misattribution invalidates both
options.misconception: treats a two-part claim as one indivisible fact

options.text: The tree-ring chronology is unreliable, since a growth anomaly that has been dated to the wrong event cannot be used to date anything
options.misconception: condemns a method on the ground of one misattribution

options.text: The report has settled the question, since three candidates and a secure date leave only one plausible choice among them
options.misconception: mistakes a reduction in uncertainty for a resolution of it

options.text: The date was the more secure part of the old claim and the attribution the weaker, so a chemical test can remove an anchor without moving a chronology, leaving a smaller set of candidates rather than a new date

questions.explanation: The report is a clean example of a claim with two parts being corrected in one part, and the discipline is to see the two parts separately. A growth anomaly in a tree is dated by the ring series it sits in, and that date does not depend on which volcano erupted, so the chronology survives the reassignment intact. What the chemistry changes is the meaning of the event: the deposit is a different volcano, and therefore a different wind, a different latitude and a different climatic footprint, which is precisely what the ice-core dating was supposed to supply. The most interesting outcome is the last sentence, because removing one candidate from a short list of a few is a large gain in precision and it also shows how much of the apparent certainty in the old account rested on an identification nobody had tested. That is the general lesson, and it is worth more than the specific case.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the old claim the chemical test bears on, and which part it leaves untouched.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: One measurement and two ranges
questions.learningObjective: explain why a dated event can have two equally supported answers
questions.stem: A single sample from the destruction layer of a trading port is dated, and the laboratory returns one radiocarbon age, from which the calibration gives two calendar ranges: one with a little over a third of the probability and another with about a quarter, separated by a gap of years, and no further information to choose between them. Which statement about that result is best supported?

options.text: The laboratory has made an error, since one measurement cannot properly produce two answers
options.misconception: assumes a one-to-one mapping between a measurement and a date

options.text: The two ranges show that the sample was contaminated, since contamination produces exactly this pattern
options.misconception: attaches a laboratory cause to a property of the curve

options.text: The shape of the calibration curve at that period is responsible, since a flat section of the curve maps one measured age onto two widely separated calendar intervals
The wider of the two ranges should be reported, since a wider interval is the more cautious statement of a result
options.misconception: confuses reporting a bimodal result with rounding it into one interval

questions.explanation: The curve is the whole of the explanation, and the reason is worth stating carefully because it is counter-intuitive. The calibration curve is built by measuring dated material of known calendar age and plotting its measured radiocarbon age against its true year, and the curve is not a straight line: it rises, flattens, and rises again, because the amount of carbon in the atmosphere has not varied smoothly. On a flat stretch, a given measured age is consistent with a long stretch of real years, and where the curve turns sharply, a small change in the measurement produces a large change in the calendar age, so a single measurement can come out as two separated clusters of plausible years. That is what a two-peaked calibrated result is reporting, and the correct response is to report both, with their probabilities, rather than to choose one or to average them into a single figure that corresponds to no year at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the calibration curve looks like at that period, and what a flat part of it does to a measurement.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A cargo that fixes the recipe
questions.learningObjective: compute a metal's composition from a stated ratio
questions.stem: A shipwreck of the late Bronze Age carried, among much else, copper and tin ingots in the ratio of about ten parts copper to one part tin, which is the recipe for the alloy those kingdoms made. If a founder had 1,100 kilograms of that alloy, how many kilograms of tin would it contain?

options.text: 1,000 kilograms, since the ten parts are taken to be the tin rather than the copper, and ten elevenths of 1,100 is 1,000
options.misconception: takes the larger of the two shares as the metal being asked for

options.text: 100 kilograms, since ten parts copper and one part tin is eleven parts in all and one eleventh of 1,100 is 100
110 kilograms, since a tenth of the whole is applied where the ratio gives one part in eleven
options.misconception: applies a tenth of the total where the ratio requires an eleventh

options.text: 1,100 kilograms, since the figure given is the weight of the tin before any of it was combined with the copper
options.misconception: treats the weight of the alloy as the weight of the tin

questions.explanation: A ratio of parts has to be turned into a total before anything can be calculated from it, and that is the only real difficulty here. Ten parts of copper to one part of tin is eleven equal parts in the whole, so the tin is one of eleven equal shares, and 1,100 divided by 11 is 100. The three wrong answers are each produced by a specific and common slip rather than chosen at random. Taking the ten parts as the tin gives 1,000, since ten elevenths of 1,100 is 1,000, and that is the error of reading a ratio without asking which of the two numbers the small share belongs to. Applying a tenth of the whole gives 110, which would be right if the ratio were already expressed as a percentage of the total, but a ratio between the two metals has the sum of the two shares as its denominator. And 1,100 is the weight of the alloy as it stands, before the tin and the copper were combined, which is the error of reading a question about one constituent as though it asked about the mixture. The alloy's composition is also why the wreck matters: a cargo of ingots is evidence of a supply chain rather than of a technique.
questions.hint: Ask how many equal parts the ratio makes in the whole, and take one of them.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A site is not a society
questions.learningObjective: state what a settlement's remains can and cannot stand for
questions.stem: A single settlement yields a great quantity of material: pottery, animal bone, seeds, iron tools, and the foundations of a large number of houses, and a study reports from it that the society of which it was a part was stratified, agricultural, and highly organised. Which statement about that claim is best supported?

options.text: The material is consistent with such a society but cannot establish it, since a settlement is one place, one section of a population, and a moment, and the people who lived elsewhere are not in it
The claim is established, since a large quantity of material from one well-excavated settlement is a fair sample of the society that produced it
options.misconception: infers representativeness from quantity alone

options.text: The claim is impossible, since nothing can be known about a society from the ground it stood on
options.misconception: converts a limit into a prohibition

options.text: The claim is established for the economy and not for the politics, since tools show labour and houses show families but neither shows a state
options.misconception: divides the claim by material type and settles the halves by assumption

questions.explanation: The generalisation from a site to a society has to be argued for, and the argument can be made, but the study as described has not made it. Three separate gaps stand between the material and the claim. The site is one place, and a society may include settlements of several kinds, of which a large town is one. It is a section of a population, since the people who were not buried there, did not live there, or lived in a household that left no trace are absent from it. And it is a moment, since a single occupation phase is a snapshot whose duration is usually short. Each gap can be closed by survey and by comparison, which is what a regional programme does, and until it is closed the honest formulation is that the finds are consistent with the description, which is a real and useful finding and a different thing from a demonstration.
questions.hint: Ask what proportion of a society could be present at one excavated settlement, and for how long.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The excavated part
questions.learningObjective: explain the inference a large excavation licenses and the one it does not
questions.stem: A long-running excavation has opened a substantial fraction of one large settlement, and a study concludes from it that the settlement was a market town, since the excavated area contains buildings used for storage, for craft production and for trade. Which statement about that conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The conclusion holds for the whole settlement, since a settlement is functionally uniform and any part of it can stand for the rest
options.misconception: assumes uniformity that a large town plainly lacks

options.text: The conclusion cannot be established even for the excavated area, since the function of a building is never more than a guess
options.misconception: denies that a building's use can be inferred at all

options.text: The conclusion is a statement about a market economy, since storage, craft and trade buildings are proof of the exchange system that produced them
options.misconception: reads a set of functions as a whole economic system

options.text: The functions are established for the excavated area, and the conclusion holds for the whole settlement if the excavated area was chosen without regard to function, which the study should therefore state

questions.explanation: A large excavation is genuinely powerful and its power comes from a specific condition that the study has to establish rather than assume. Where a large fraction of a settlement has been opened and the sample was not chosen because of what it might contain, the absence of a function from the excavated area becomes evidence about the settlement as a whole, and that is what makes a large excavation different from a small one. It is a strong argument, and it is worth being explicit that it is an argument about the absence of things, which is much weaker than an argument about their presence. The fourth option is the mistake of moving a level up, from a set of buildings with certain uses to a claim about a whole economy, and the second is the mistake of assuming homogeneity, which is exactly what a large town denies. Both are common and both are avoidable by saying which level the claim is at.
questions.hint: Ask how the excavated area was chosen, since that decides what the absence of a function means.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A field visible only from the air
questions.learningObjective: explain what an aerial method can and cannot establish
questions.stem: An aerial survey of a cultivated plain finds faint marks visible as differences in the colour of the crop, and follow-up on the ground confirms that they sit above buried ditches and banks. A further survey of forest finds nothing, and a study concludes that the forest contains no archaeology. Which statement about the second conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The conclusion is sound, since a field that cannot be seen cannot be there
options.misconception: identifies invisibility with absence

options.text: The conclusion is sound, since the plain's fields prove the method works, so the method is reliable everywhere
options.misconception: extends a validation in one setting to all settings

options.text: The method detects differences in the surface, and a forest canopy removes the surface, so a negative result there is a statement about the method rather than about the ground
The forest should be cleared before the survey, since the absence of a canopy is a precondition of detection rather than a limitation on it
options.misconception: confuses a condition of the method with a solution to it

questions.explanation: An aerial method reads a difference in the appearance of the ground surface, and what produces that difference is a matter of what happens to lie beneath it: a ditch holds different moisture, a bank drains differently, a wall changes how deep a plough cuts, and a filled-in pit grows a different crop. Remove the surface and the signal goes with it, so a survey over woodland, dunes, marsh or deep alluvium returns a blank that means nothing at all about what is underneath. This is the general problem of a negative result from a remote method, and the responsible way to state it is to bound the conclusion by the conditions under which the method can work. The case is instructive because the first survey both succeeded and was confirmed on the ground, so the failure in the second place is a change of conditions rather than a change of method, and that distinction is exactly what a reader has to be able to make.
questions.hint: Ask what the method actually senses, and whether that thing is present in the second landscape.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A single collapse in a modern narrative
questions.learningObjective: assess a conventional date whose convenience is suspect
questions.stem: A review of recent work on the end of the Bronze Age in the eastern Mediterranean observes that the idea of a single collapse marked by a widespread destruction horizon is debated, that going back to the original reports and tracing the citation chains back from the claimed destructions shows that much of the standard account is an artefact of scholarship, and that in the absence of evidence a destruction should not be dated where a ready-made narrative would like it. Which reading of the review is best supported?

options.text: The review is calling for the coincidence to be demonstrated rather than assumed, since a date that fits an existing story will be found for events that were never shown to belong together
The review is denying that the palaces ended, since a doubt about the simultaneity of the destructions is a doubt about the destructions themselves
options.misconception: converts a claim about synchronism into a claim about occurrence

options.text: The review is proposing a new date, since the dates the tracing produced must have been later than the conventional one
options.misconception: supplies a replacement figure the review does not give

options.text: The review is establishing that the earlier scholars were mistaken, since citation tracing can establish what a claim was based on and therefore whether it was founded
options.misconception: confuses tracing a citation with refuting its content

questions.explanation: The warning is about the interaction between a chronology and a narrative, and it is a real hazard because the two are usually built together. Once a model says a whole region failed in a single generation, individual destructions acquire a date by being read as members of that event, and a destruction that can be dated only loosely is then given a date that makes it fit. Tracing the citations back shows how many of the synchronisms are in fact a single early claim repeated by later writers, which is a legitimate finding about the literature and not by itself a finding about the past. The disciplined conclusion is the one the review reaches: the coincidence has to be demonstrated from the sites rather than assumed, and where it cannot be demonstrated, the account of a single collapse is a hypothesis about the literature at least as much as about the Bronze Age. The third option supplies a date the review does not offer.
questions.hint: Ask how a destruction gets its date, and what happens when the date makes it fit a story.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A claim that the ruins were built by strangers
questions.learningObjective: assess an attribution of a monument to an outside origin
questions.stem: A large stone city is described by a nineteenth-century visitor in a report that attributes its buildings to a people who came from far away and left no trace in the country, on the ground that a local population could not have built it. The visitor's own account also records that families were living inside the walls at the time of the visit and that they used a local name for the place. Which statement about the attribution is best supported?

options.text: The attribution follows from the size of the walls, since a structure on that scale cannot have been raised by a small population
options.misconception: infers an outside workforce from a structure's size

options.text: The attribution is settled by the absence of written records, since a people who left none cannot be identified with the builders
options.misconception: uses an absence of records as evidence about builders

options.text: The attribution is a claim that needs evidence of its own, and the account supplies a reason to doubt it in the fact that local families were living in the buildings and naming the place
The attribution is a matter of taste, since several accounts of the site are equally consistent with the evidence
options.misconception: reduces an evidential question to preference

questions.explanation: A claim about who built something is an ordinary historical claim and has to be argued like one, and the difficulty here is that the argument is circular in a way that is easy to miss. If the buildings are remarkable, and if the population living among them is assumed to be of a different kind, then the builders must have been others; but the assumption about the population is precisely what the buildings are being used to establish. The fact recorded in the same account, that families were living inside the walls and had a name for the place, is not a small detail to be set aside, because it is a record of continuous occupation and local naming by the people the claim sets outside the story. An attribution of this kind is best treated as a hypothesis to be tested against the material found on the site, and a great deal of weight then falls on the pottery, the tools and the animal bone, since those are the things a foreign origin has to explain away.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence would have to be produced for a foreign origin, and whether the report produced any.

questions.topic: The claim that was reversed on the ground
questions.learningObjective: trace how a conclusion about a site was overturned
questions.stem: A scholar working in the early twentieth century examined the finds at a great stone city, compared them with the finds of the period, and concluded that the city was medieval and the work of the people living in the country. Which feature of that conclusion is most likely to have decided it?

options.text: The absence of a written record, since a site with no inscriptions is thereby a site with no date
options.misconception: uses silence as a date

options.text: The material itself, since a comparison of the pottery, the tools and the iron at the site with dated material elsewhere puts the occupation inside a period that is now dated
The size of the walls, since construction on that scale requires a state that only one region is known to have had
options.misconception: infers a builder from a structure's size

options.text: The presence of local families living in the ruins, since occupation without a record is the mark of a people without a history
options.misconception: repeats the circular inference it is supposed to settle

questions.explanation: The reversal of a long-standing attribution is one of the most instructive episodes in the subject, and it was achieved by the least rhetorical method available, which is dating the things that were found. A city cannot be assigned a period by its appearance; it can be assigned one by the pottery, the metalwork and the animal bone recovered from it, compared with the same materials from sites whose dates are independently established. When that comparison places the occupation inside a period that can be dated, and when the objects resemble those of the people living in the country rather than those of any tradition brought from elsewhere, the attribution follows without anyone having to argue about the character of a people. This is why the episode matters beyond its own case: a claim about a whole civilisation was overturned by a table of finds, and the reason it had lasted so long is that it answered a question about identity that the finds could test and that its supporters never tested them against.
questions.hint: Ask what the material from the site was compared with, and what the comparison decided.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An excavation that removed what it was measuring
questions.learningObjective: assess the loss an excavation causes to the evidence it studies
questions.stem: A curator was appointed to a great stone site with a written mandate to preserve the building, and he spent three years clearing debris from the inside of the walls, moving what he described as waste, in order that the architecture might be seen and photographed. A later archaeologist wrote that the work left only vestiges of the deposits within the walls, and a paucity that would inhibit all future work. Which statement about the clearing is soundest?

options.text: The clearing was a destruction of the site, since nothing about a building's preservation requires the removal of anything at all
options.misconception: makes preservation and archaeology identical and indicts the whole discipline

options.text: The clearing was correct, since the deposits had been recorded before the work began and the architecture was the monument of interest
options.misconception: assumes a prior record the case does not mention

options.text: The clearing was a necessary preliminary, since a site cannot be studied at all until the deposits covering it have been removed
options.misconception: treats one method's necessity as the necessity of stripping every site

options.text: The clearing was a reasonable act of conservation answered with a method that destroyed the evidence, since a deposit inside a wall is a record of use and removing it as waste removes the record of the site's history

questions.explanation: This is a case where the two aims were genuinely good and the method was genuinely wrong, and it is worth holding onto precisely because the conflict is not between conservation and knowledge but between two ways of serving the same end. The mandate was to preserve a building, and a building half-buried in debris is not legible as architecture, so clearing has a real justification; but the deposits inside those walls are the stratified record of who used the site, when, and for what, and they are removed in exactly the order that destroys the sequence, from the top down. The damage is irreversible in a way that matters more than for a lost object, because a lost object can be recorded and photographed while a lost deposit cannot be re-excavated later with the stratigraphy intact. The general lesson is the one the occupation of the site makes vivid: a site is a monument and a set of deposits at once, and a plan that protects the first has to be designed so that it does not consume the second.
questions.hint: Ask what the debris consisted of, and what a sequence means once it has been dug out from the top.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A number that the sources do not agree on
questions.learningObjective: assess a disputed count and the reason the sources differ
questions.stem: The number of objects removed from a palace in the nineteenth century is given in the published literature as between about two thousand and about five thousand, and in one recent provenance study as more than ten thousand. An eyewitness account given to a parliamentary committee states that the objects were not catalogued when taken, that the men who looted the palace did the cataloguing afterwards, and that the count is derived from those soldiers' accounts. Which statement about the figures is best supported?

options.text: The largest figure should be preferred, since a count made by eye underestimates and a later study with records should be closer to the truth
options.misconception: prefers a larger number on the ground that bigger is better informed

options.text: The figures are reconcilable, since each counts a different class of object and together they give a total
options.misconception: assumes the differences are a partition rather than a disagreement

options.text: The figures measure different things and the disagreement is itself the finding, since a count assembled afterwards by the people who took the objects is evidence about their accounts rather than about the holdings of the palace
No figure can be used, since a count nobody agrees on cannot support any statement about what was removed
options.misconception: refuses all use where the spread itself is informative

questions.explanation: The committee's witness is describing a failure of record-keeping that occurred at a particular moment and has consequences for everything downstream. The objects were not inventoried when they were taken, so the first count was made afterwards from memory, from what was sold, and from what turned up in dealers' hands years later, and each of those channels has its own bias; the men who looted had an interest in understating what they had taken and in keeping quiet about what they had sold on. That is a reason to expect a spread, and it is also a reason to read the spread as evidence about the process rather than as noise to be averaged. A disagreement of this kind is still usable: it constrains the true figure to an order of magnitude, it shows that a single summary number would be false precision, and the disagreement itself documents the absence of any contemporaneous inventory, which is itself a fact about how the event was conducted.
questions.hint: Ask who made the count, and when, and what they were counting from.

stimulus.body: From a paper read to the guild of metalworkers and entered in the court's records: 'Concerning the metal cast for the palace. This metal is not found in this country, nor in any country to the north of it, and the smiths hold that they have never seen it come out of a stone here, though they have seen the ore brought from the north and roasted without success. It arrives out the sea in the ships, in bars, and the captain of a ship names the port at which his cargo was loaded and the house that shipped it. The guild was pressed this quarter for a greater weight than the ships brought, and the answer returned is that the ships bring what they bring. The palace has therefore the metal and the work, and it has neither the ore nor the road.'

questions.stem: Read the report. A kingdom in the forest region of West Africa produced a large body of cast brass plaques and heads showing its court, its ancestors and its wars. Which inference follows from the two facts together?

options.text: The kingdom's metalworking depended on imported material, so its art is evidence of a supply system and a court that commanded one, and the objects carry information about the trade that produced them
The kingdom's art was necessarily inferior, since a metal that had to be imported could not be worked to the standard seen in the objects
options.misconception: judges quality by the origin of the raw material

options.text: The objects must be copies of work made elsewhere, since the metal's origin fixes the place the objects were made
options.misconception: assumes a material's origin determines a workshop's location

options.text: The kingdom cannot have had a metallurgical tradition of its own, since a tradition requires a domestic source of ore
options.misconception: equates a tradition with self-sufficiency in raw material

questions.explanation: The combination of a sophisticated body of objects and a region without the raw material is one of the most useful kinds of evidence there is, because it forces a specific inference about connections rather than about quality. The report adds the detail that makes the point sharp, since the metal comes as bars named by a port and a shipping house, so the objects are downstream of a transaction that somebody else had to agree to. The three distractors are each a familiar error in reverse, and the last is the one to watch: no tradition requires domestic ore, and the societies that built the most impressive metalwork on imported metal are numerous.
questions.hint: Ask what the report says about the source of the metal, and what the objects' own quality says about the workshops.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An inventory kept in the things themselves
questions.learningObjective: explain how objects can function as records
questions.stem: A court records its history not in a written chronicle but in cast plaques and ivory pendants that show named ancestors, particular campaigns, particular events, and the regalia worn at a person's installation in office, and the right to wear an item is granted by the ruler. Which statement about the evidentiary value of that arrangement is best supported?

options.text: The objects are decoration, since a court that records its history in objects is a court without written institutions
options.misconception: equates the absence of one technology with the absence of record-keeping

options.text: The objects are records, since an image of a named event placed in a public place and re-cast for a new reign is evidence that somebody wanted a particular version of that event on permanent display
The objects are unusable, since images of events cannot be checked against anything and a picture is not a document
options.misconception: assumes images cannot be corroborated at all

options.text: The objects are records of a different society, since they were made for export and so describe the buyers rather than the makers
options.misconception: supposes a market that the case does not mention

questions.explanation: The arrangement described is a record-keeping technology, and identifying it as one is the whole point of the item. A named ancestor cast in metal and installed in a palace is a claim about history made in a durable medium, and the fact that a later ruler re-cast the series for his own reign is itself a fact about the politics: the record is a statement of what the reigning house holds to be true and worth perpetuating. Where an object's use is controlled by the ruler, the object's circulation is a record of office as well, since who may wear what and when is a chronology of appointments. None of this makes the record neutral, and the biases are systematic and predictable, which is what makes a record usable once its bias is known. An object that cannot be compared with anything else is still evidence of a belief held and expressed; one that can be compared with a written list becomes a check on that list.
questions.hint: Ask what it means to re-cast a series for a new reign, and what a record that is deliberately placed can still show.
