questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission that asked the wrong question
questions.learningObjective: assess the framing of a research commission
questions.stem: Objects taken from a palace are described in the nineteenth-century literature as works of primitive art, and a commission reporting on them states that the people who made them did not produce them for galleries and museums but for their own court, and that the objects are the record of a dynastic and political history. Which statement about the commission's finding is best supported?

options.text: The finding is a correction of a date, since showing that the objects record a dynastic history moves them to a later period than they had been assigned
options.misconception: turns a change of description into a change of date

options.text: The finding is an aesthetic judgement, since objects made for a purpose other than display are by that fact less accomplished
options.misconception: converts a functional claim into a ranking of quality

options.text: The finding is a restatement of the objects' subject matter, since showing a history is depicted is the same as showing it was recorded
options.misconception: equates depicting a thing with recording it

options.text: The finding is a correction of a category rather than a correction of a date, since it establishes what kind of object the things are, and a description of kind is prior to any historical use of them

questions.explanation: The commission's intervention is a change of category, and changes of category are prior in an unusual way because they determine what questions an object can be asked. Once the objects are called works of art made for a market, the interesting questions become questions of style, comparison and attribution, and the material in front of the reader is treated as a set of objects without users. Once they are palace fittings, a court workshop's product and a record of office, the same material becomes evidence about a hierarchy of people, about campaigns, about the sequence of reigns, and about who was authorised to wear what. Nothing about the physical objects has changed, and no date has moved, but the number of historical questions available has changed completely. That is why the category is not a matter of taste, and why the term used for the objects in the earlier literature is itself part of the record a historian has to notice.
questions.hint: Ask what changes about the available questions when an object is reclassified, and what does not change.

questions.topic: The text that names the site
questions.learningObjective: assess a colonial report as a historical source
questions.stem: The first published account of a great stone site in southern Africa was written by a man whose object was to establish who had built it, and it reports a local population's account of the place alongside his own conclusion that the buildings could not have been raised by them. The local account is recorded because it was useful to his argument and is generally regarded as less reliable than his own observations. Which statement about that judgement is best supported?

options.text: The judgement is sound, since an account given to a traveller who disbelieves it is by that fact unreliable
options.misconception: judges a report's reliability by the listener's reaction to it

options.text: The judgement is reversed by the later evidence, since a claim recorded by someone who was going to use it is still a record of what the people he met said, and it can be tested against the material as well as against his conclusion
The judgement is sound, since the traveller spent years at the site and the people he asked had no written record to check
options.misconception: rewards length of residence and ignores the reason for the doubt

options.text: The judgement is reversed, since an eyewitness report always outranks a report compiled by later travellers
options.misconception: asserts a general precedence between kinds of testimony

questions.explanation: The judgement here is a bad one, and the reason it is bad is generalizable. A report of what somebody said is evidence about what that person said, and the fact that the reporter disbelieved it, or benefited from disbelieving it, or found it convenient is a fact about the reporter's reliability on other matters rather than a reason to discard the report. The right response is to hold the report at arm's length and test it, and the test in this case is unusually available, since the material culture of the site is exactly the sort of thing against which a local claim about who built it can be checked. This is a case where a hostile record turns out to be one of the best sources available, and the practical lesson for a reader is to ask what a source was doing rather than whether it agrees with the story one already believes.
questions.hint: Ask what the local account is evidence of, and what the reporter's disagreement shows about him.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order in which a site's history was reassessed
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which an attribution was reversed
questions.stem: A long-standing claim about who built a great stone city was reversed during the twentieth century. The steps that produced the reversal are set out below. Place them in the order in which they happened.

options.text: The finds recovered from the site, including pottery, iron and worked stone, were compared with dated material from elsewhere and placed within a datable period
A working party with a mandate to preserve the building cleared debris from inside the walls, and the deposits were removed without being recorded in section
A traveller's published account of the site attributed the buildings to a people from elsewhere, and that attribution was accepted for decades
Researchers on the site concluded that the buildings belong within a period and a cultural tradition of the people of the country, which contradicted the published attribution

questions.explanation: The order runs from the claim to the evidence to the conclusion, and the clearing is last for a reason the case supplies. The traveler's attribution comes first because a published claim is what a later study has to confront, and for several decades it went unchallenged, which is itself a fact about the state of the subject. The comparison of finds comes second, and it is the step that does the work, since a comparison with dated material places the occupation in a period and a tradition without anyone's having to argue about a people's character. The conclusion follows from the comparison, and the clearing comes after because the deposits that would have strengthened it further were removed without being recorded, so the last step is a loss that happened once the central question had already been answered by other evidence and which limits what can be settled afterwards. The sequence is a compact model of how a subject revises itself: claim, evidence, revision, cost.
questions.hint: Ask what the later work had to confront first, and what it used to decide the question.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A kingdom's script that few can read
questions.learningObjective: assess what a surviving script does and does not preserve

stimulus.body: From a report laid before a learned society on the inscriptions of a Nile kingdom: 'Of the texts brought down from the temples and the tombs, a small number carry the names of kings with their titles, and to those alone we have attained a reading. The remainder, some thousands of short inscriptions scratched on pots, on plastered walls and on the steps of the temples, are set out in a script whose signs we can enumerate and whose words we cannot follow, the tongue they record being one we cannot identify. It should not be concluded that this kingdom wrote less than its neighbours did, for of all the writing of this period it is ours that we understand least. Of what these texts were for we can say only that their cutters expected something of them, since the shortest are cut where a man must stand close to read them.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the report. Which statement about the kingdom's written record is best supported?

options.text: The kingdom wrote extensively and the writing is largely lost to us, so the silence of the record is a fact about the decipherment and not about the kingdom's activity
The kingdom wrote little, since a kingdom that produced a great many inscriptions would have produced enough of them for scholars to read
options.misconception: infers the amount of writing from the ability to read it

options.text: The inscriptions describe only what the kingdom wished outsiders to know, so the unread ones are unpromising as a source
options.misconception: supposes a motive for a whole body of material

options.text: The kingdom's history is unrecoverable, since history consists of what can be read and this cannot be read
options.misconception: treats unread records as no records

questions.explanation: A language that survives in a script nobody has cracked is a very different situation from a kingdom that wrote nothing, and the difference is worth being exact about because the first is often described in the words appropriate to the second. The inscriptions are still there, in their hundreds, in their original setting, in the buildings where they were displayed, and the script itself is legible as a script even where the language is not. What is missing is a bridge, and a bridge is the kind of thing that can be built: a readable text in a related language, a bilingual inscription, a long text with enough internal repetition to be a dictionary, or a proper noun that appears in a source in another language. Meanwhile the quantities alone carry information, since a kingdom that produced this much writing was doing something regular with it, and the places where the inscriptions stand are a map of where the kingdom chose to be seen. The silence is in the decipherment, and the item is testing whether a reader can locate the silence correctly.
questions.hint: Ask whether the absence is in the writing or in our reading of it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A text that was copied and recopied
questions.learningObjective: explain what transmission does to a text
questions.stem: A work survives in a single manuscript copied several centuries after it was written, and a comparison of that manuscript with fragments of earlier copies shows that the earlier copies agreed with one another in a passage where the surviving manuscript differs. Which statement about the passage is best supported?

options.text: The passage is the original reading, since the later manuscript is a copy and a copy follows its exemplar
options.misconception: assumes a copy preserves what its exemplar had

options.text: The passage cannot be assessed, since a comparison of copies establishes only that they differ
options.misconception: misses what a majority of earlier copies is evidence about

options.text: The passage is a later addition to the original work, since the earlier copies were made by scribes who did not read the whole text
options.misconception: confuses a variation with a structural addition

options.text: The passage is a later alteration, since the earlier agreement makes the surviving reading the exception and the copyists' choice is the change

questions.explanation: A single surviving manuscript has no authority over the work it transmits, because it is one witness among a tradition and the tradition's earlier members are evidence about what the text said. Where two or more earlier copies agree against the survivor, the ordinary reading is that the survivor's scribe made a change, and the change is a datum: it tells us that something about the passage invited improvement, or confusion, or an attempt to make it mean something else, which is often more interesting than the text would have been otherwise. The discipline is to keep the two questions apart, which is what the fourth option does not: whether a passage is original and whether the work has a later structural addition are different problems with different evidence, and a variant reading is evidence for the first and not for the second.
questions.hint: Ask which witnesses are earlier, and what their agreement does to the reading.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A date that a ship supplied
questions.learningObjective: explain how one object can date a whole sequence
questions.stem: A wreck that sank with a dated cargo of objects aboard, in a region where the same kinds of objects are found in dated burials, is used to date a group of sites whose own material cannot be dated independently. Which statement about that use is best supported?

options.text: The wreck dates the burials exactly, since the objects came from the same makers and a maker's work has a single date
options.misconception: assumes a style or a workshop has one date

options.text: The wreck has no bearing on the burials, since a thing that sank in one place cannot tell us about a burial in another
options.misconception: denies the possibility of a comparative date

options.text: The wreck supplies an external fixed point, so the objects in the burials can be placed relative to it, provided the connection between the burial objects and the cargo is argued rather than assumed
The wreck dates the region rather than the burials, since a dated cargo dates the whole culture that produced it
options.misconception: generalises a single object's date to a culture

questions.explanation: A securely dated find is one of the most valuable things a region can acquire, and the mechanism is comparison rather than connection. The wreck gives an assemblage of objects with a date that is independent of anything on land, and a burial assemblage that contains the same kinds of material can be placed on the same footing provided the overlap is real and the differences are understood. The word doing the work in the correct option is argued, because the connection between a cargo and a burial assemblage can fail in several ordinary ways: the objects may be older than the wreck, the burial may be much later than either, and the two may share only a coarse category. This is the ordinary way most regional chronologies are built, not through absolute dates for every site but through a network of overlaps anchored on a small number of firm points, and it is why a single well-dated wreck can reorganise the dating of a whole region.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the wreck's date firm, and what would have to be shown about the burials' contents.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A count made by a conqueror
questions.learningObjective: assess a figure recorded by an occupying power

stimulus.body: From the return of the officer appointed to take the census of a country newly brought under a conquering administration, made in the twelfth month of the first year of the conquest: 'By district, of hearths: the first, four thousand one hundred and twenty; the second, two thousand eight hundred and eighty; the third, one thousand and fifty. I certify the enumeration was made in person at every settlement and by the same rule in every district. I further report that in the third district the greater part of those who formerly lived in the open villages have gone up into the hills or over the frontier, and that the enumeration of the same district ten years before returned six thousand seven hundred. In the second district the sickness of the last summer is said to have carried off a great part of the adults.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the return. The figure for the country is used for two centuries in computing the growth rate of the region. Which statement about it is best supported?

options.text: The figure is the one early observation that exists, and it is best used as a fixed point whose uncertainty is stated rather than as the first term of a series, since the conquest itself changed who was counted and who was missing
The figure is unusable, since a return written by a conqueror has an interest in the number it reports
options.misconception: rejects a document on the ground of the writer's interest and nothing else

options.text: The figure is the most reliable of all later figures, since the conquering administration had better information than anyone who came before it
options.misconception: assumes a conqueror's information is better for counting

options.text: The figure is reliable if the conquerors intended to tax the population, since a taxpayer's count is checked against the tax actually collected
options.misconception: assumes a motive that would make the count accurate, without evidence

The reasons are ordinary and unremarkable. People had gone to the hills and over the frontier, which is what happens to a settled population under conquest, and a sickness had carried off a large share of the adults in one district, which is a demographic shock rather than a counting error. The fourth option names a genuinely useful idea, since a count tied to a tax is checked against something independent, but nothing in the return says these hearths were taxed, and a tax count is checked for revenue reasons rather than for demographic ones.
questions.hint: Ask what the conquest did to who was living there, and what a first observation can be used for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conclusion drawn from an absence
questions.learningObjective: assess an argument from missing evidence
questions.stem: A study argues that a kingdom's population was small, because almost no human burials have been found at its sites, while burials are plentiful at the sites of a neighbouring kingdom of the same size and period. A second study argues that the first kingdom buried its dead inside houses, and that such burials are difficult to detect in excavation. Which statement about the pair is soundest?

options.text: The first argument rests on a difference in burial practice, and the second identifies the specific feature of the record that would have to be searched for directly before the absence can be read as a small population
The second study is right that the population was small, since houses cannot hold a burial and a kingdom that buried inside houses must have had few of them
options.misconception: infers a population from a burial practice in the wrong direction

options.text: The two studies are incompatible, since one claims a small population and the other does not address population at all
options.misconception: manufactures a disagreement between a claim and a qualification

options.text: The first argument is unaffected, since a kingdom of a given size has a fixed number of burials whatever it does with its dead
options.misconception: assumes a fixed burial rate independent of practice

questions.explanation: An argument from absence is only as strong as the completeness of the record, and the second study's contribution is to name precisely where the record is thin. Burial practice is one of the strongest controls on what survives: a cemetery of stone graves is easy to locate and easy to date, a cremation is hard to date, and a burial inside a house leaves a trace that a digger has to be told to look for and that can be destroyed by later occupation of the same floor. So the absence at the first kingdom's sites is exactly what would be expected if its practice were the one described, and the inference from the absence to a small population loses its foundation. That does not establish a large population either, and the honest next step is the one the second study names: a search designed for the kind of trace the practice leaves. The general rule is that an absence in the archaeological record is a fact about deposition, preservation and detection, and only after all three have been ruled out is it a fact about the past.
questions.hint: Ask what feature of the record would be missing, and whether anyone has looked for it.

questions.topic: A drought that left no trace of its own
questions.learningObjective: explain how a cause is inferred when it leaves no direct signal
questions.stem: A study attributes the decline of a group of settlements to a drought, on the ground that the settlements lie in a basin whose water supply depends on a lake, that the lake's level is reconstructed from its sediments, that the reconstruction shows a fall coinciding with the decline, and that a population whose water comes from a falling lake must move. Which feature of that reasoning is weakest?

options.text: The sediment reconstruction is a measurement rather than an interpretation, so the dating of the lake level is the only part of the argument that can be questioned
options.misconception: accepts a proxy without question and questions only its date

options.text: The coincidence of the two series is itself proof of the connection, since two unrelated changes do not coincide by chance
options.misconception: asserts that coincidence excludes chance

options.text: The chain from a falling lake to a move depends on people having no alternative to that lake, and the case has not shown that the settlements had no other source or that they moved rather than coping
The argument is sound in its parts and sound in its conclusion, since each step in it is independently established
options.misconception: conflates the establishment of each step with the establishment of the whole

questions.explanation: Every step of a causal chain in this field has to be earned, and the last one before the conclusion is usually the one that is skipped. Knowing that a lake fell and knowing that a settlement declined in the same century is real evidence, and the physical mechanism connecting them is plausible, which is why the case is worth making. What is missing is the behavioural step: a settlement beside a falling lake may move, may dig, may change what it grows, may eat differently, or may do nothing at all, and these responses have very different consequences for the archaeological record, since only one of them produces abandonment. The fourth option names a real and common error, that a chain whose links are individually established has thereby been established, which is true of a deductive chain and not of this one, where each link is a probabilistic inference and the whole is weaker than its parts. The honest conclusion is a mechanism requiring a behavioural assumption that has to be evidenced.
questions.hint: Ask what people beside a falling lake can do other than leave, and whether the case has shown they had no choice.

questions.topic: A choice to adapt rather than to abandon
questions.learningObjective: read an archaeological response as a decision rather than a failure
questions.stem: Along a coast whose sea level rose over several centuries, a study finds that some sites were inundated and abandoned while others in the same region were reworked: ditches were dug, ground was built up, and cultivation was moved into wetland that had not previously been farmed. Which of the following follow from that pattern? Select all that apply.

options.text: The region contained both a decision to move and a decision to stay and rework, so the difference between the two outcomes lies in the choices made and the resources available rather than in the change itself
The reworked sites show that the people there treated a rising sea as a problem to be solved at a cost, rather than as a condition that had to be obeyed
The reworked sites show that the work was unnecessary, since the sea eventually rose past them as well
options.misconception: judges the effort by an outcome it could not have known

options.text: The abandonment of the inundated sites shows that the region lacked the labour to adapt anywhere, since two adjacent groups faced one change
options.misconception: infers a region-wide shortage from two different outcomes

options.text: The wetland cultivation shows that the people who used it had previously rejected it, since a practice abandoned is a practice not worth using
options.misconception: assumes a practice's earlier absence was a considered rejection

questions.explanation: The two defensible readings both take the divergence seriously as evidence of choice rather than as a puzzle to be smoothed away. A and B in effect say that the same change produced two outcomes, and that the useful question is what differed between the two places, which is a question about labour, tenure, the productivity of the new land, and the distance a household had to move. Taking adaptation seriously also changes the moral register of a collapse narrative, because an adaptation that was tried and then overwhelmed is a different event from an abandonment that was the only option, and the record can usually distinguish them. The third option applies a judgement no one at the time could have made. The fourth mistakes a difference in outcome for a difference in capacity. The fifth reads a practice's absence as a decision, when the ordinary reason a wetland is not farmed is that it is not yet worth farming.
questions.hint: Ask what the two groups of sites were doing differently, and what that says about the change itself.

questions.topic: An end and a beginning
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the end of a form of government from the end of a tradition
questions.stem: The city-states of the southern lowlands of one region stop building monuments and stop cutting dated inscriptions in the ninth century, and a century later the cities to the north are larger and busier than they have ever been, though they carve far fewer dated stones. A study concludes that what ended was the southern city-states and not the tradition they belonged to. Which feature of the evidence supports that conclusion most directly?

options.text: The tradition continued in a different place and in a changed form, so what the southern evidence shows is the end of a distribution of power rather than the end of a way of life
The southern cities were destroyed, since a city that stops building has been destroyed
options.misconception: infers destruction from a cessation of building

options.text: The northern cities are the same cities, since a tradition that moves has not ended and the north is therefore the south
options.misconception: identifies two regions because a practice is shared

options.text: The monuments matter more than the people, since a tradition is a style of building and not a society
options.misconception: reduces a tradition to its monumental output

questions.explanation: The distinction does real work because the two claims are usually run together, and the evidence for them is different. The end of a system of government is shown by the disappearance of the institutions that made it: the dated inscriptions, the palace programmes, the territorial reach, the goods that only a court consumes. The end of a tradition is a much stronger claim and would need the tradition itself to disappear. What the northern evidence supplies is exactly the counter-case: the same practices of city life, ritual, astronomy and political display continuing, with a different monumental record, in a different place. That does not make the two regions interchangeable, and the study is careful not to say so, but it does mean the label that fits the southern evidence is a change in the distribution of power. The fourth option is the reduction this distinction exists to prevent.
questions.hint: Ask what ended in the south that did not end in the north, and name the two claims separately.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A kingdom's last dated record
questions.learningObjective: interpret a gap between the last record and the end
questions.stem: The last inscription of a Nile kingdom that can be securely dated is a century or so earlier than the date conventionally given for the kingdom's end, and the inscriptions in between are either undated or cannot yet be read. Which statement about the gap is best supported?

options.text: The gap shows that the kingdom ended a century earlier than the conventional date, since the last inscription is the last act of a living kingdom
options.misconception: treats the record's failure as the kingdom's end

options.text: The gap shows where the record fails rather than where the kingdom ended, since a kingdom does not stop writing when it stops existing and a date for an end has to be argued from something other than the last legible stone
The gap shows that the conventional date is wrong and the last inscription fixes the true one, since a dated record cannot be out of date
options.misconception: assumes a record is made at the moment it is dated

options.text: The gap shows that the kingdom continued, since a kingdom that outlived its own inscriptions must have been restored later
options.misconception: infers restoration from a documentary silence

questions.explanation: A record's last legible entry is a fact about legibility, and the reasons legibility fails are numerous and mostly uninteresting: the script changes, the language changes, the stone is reused, the text is too short to carry a date, the reading is disputed, or the relevant inscriptions were never found because nobody looked in the right place. None of these is evidence that the kingdom stopped, and the kingdom certainly did not stop being a kingdom because it stopped producing a text we can read. The consequence for the chronology is real, though, and it is the reverse of what the options suggest: an end date has to be established from something other than the last legible inscription, whether that is a dated reference in a neighbour's text, a change in the pottery, an occupation continuity, or an argument about the successor state, and the date that is conventionally given has usually been established on one of those grounds already. The gap marks the limit of one kind of evidence and should be reported as such.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true for a kingdom to end on the date of its last legible inscription.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A disappearance visible in a cargo
questions.learningObjective: read a change in trade goods as a change in a system
questions.stem: Wrecks of one period in a sea carry a wide range of raw materials from distant sources, and wrecks of a century or two later in the same sea carry a narrow range, with the missing categories not replaced by anything of the same kind. Which inference is best supported by that pattern?

options.text: Trade in the later period was more specialised, since a narrow range of goods is the mark of a more developed division of labour
options.misconception: reads a loss of links as a gain in sophistication

options.text: The later wrecks are better preserved, since a narrow cargo is what survives a long voyage in the best condition
options.misconception: attributes a pattern to preservation

options.text: The sea became less navigable, since a ship's master will not sail for goods the market does not want
options.misconception: supplies a navigational cause for a change in cargo

options.text: Some of the supply links that carried those goods are no longer operating, since goods disappear without being substituted, which is a different signal from a simple fall in the volume of trade

questions.explanation: The diagnostic feature is the non-substitution. A fall in the volume of trade with the same goods still present is a weak signal, since volume moves with demand, with weather, with piracy and with the number of wrecks that happened to be found. Goods that disappear from the cargoes altogether and are not replaced by substitutes are a stronger signal, because a buyer who cannot obtain tin does not switch to silver, and a state that cannot obtain copper does not simply use less bronze; the demand goes elsewhere, to different metals, different sources, or a different economy. That pattern is what a break in a supply route looks like from the seaward side, and it is one of the few places where a change in a trading system is legible in a small and reasonably unbiased sample. The second option is the seductive error, because specialisation is a praise word and this pattern deserves a second look before it is used as one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the missing goods were replaced, and what a replacement would tell you.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A destruction in a text and a destruction on the ground
questions.learningObjective: compare a literary report with an archaeological layer
questions.stem: A text of a neighbouring kingdom describes the destruction of a city and the flight of its people, and an excavation at the city's site finds a destruction layer with burnt beams and a layer of abandonment above it. Historians ask whether the two are the same event. Which statement about the comparison is soundest?

options.text: The two cannot be the same event, since a text names a place and a layer has no name, and the two can never be joined
options.misconception: denies that a layer can be identified with a place

options.text: The two must be the same event, since only one destruction is recorded in the period and the layer must belong to it
options.misconception: identifies the unique event with the described one by elimination

options.text: The two are compatible, since a burnt layer with abandonment above it is what a described sack would leave, and the work is in establishing that the dates and the circumstances match rather than in assuming that they do
The layer is the better evidence, since a burnt beam cannot be written for, so the text adds nothing to the case
options.misconception: prefers one kind of evidence and dismisses the other

questions.explanation: The comparison is the ordinary work of the subject and it is a comparison of two different things, which is why the join has to be made rather than assumed. A destruction layer establishes that a building was burnt and that the settlement was not rebuilt over a period; a text establishes that somebody burned a named place and that some people left. Neither establishes the other, and a burnt layer can be dated without a text, just as a text can be read without a layer. What the join requires is narrower than it sounds: the dates must be compatible, the scale must be compatible, the direction of the account must be compatible with the archaeology, and the alternative explanations for the layer must be excluded. The fourth option is a common error, and the reason it is wrong is that a burnt beam answers questions a text cannot and a text answers questions a burnt beam cannot, so the two are not competing for the same job.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two evidences separately, and what the join requires.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A date that was wrong for a generation
questions.learningObjective: assess the stability of a method that everybody uses
questions.stem: A widely used calibration curve is revised when a large body of new, precisely dated measurements becomes available, and a long-running debate that the previous curve had seemed to settle is reopened, because the revision shows that the older curve carried local offsets. Which statement about the situation is best supported?

options.text: The debate should not be reopened, since a settled question does not become open again because a better curve exists
options.misconception: treats a settlement as immune to better evidence

options.text: A method can be the best available for a generation and still contain an error that a later generation finds, so agreement on an answer is evidence about the evidence available rather than about the question
The revision shows that the new measurements are wrong, since a method that worked cannot have been in error for so long
options.misconception: assumes longevity is proof of correctness

options.text: The revision shows that the earlier measurements were fraudulent, since an error that persisted so long must have concealed misconduct
options.misconception: infers misconduct from a long-standing error

questions.explanation: This is the ordinary condition of a quantitative field and the reason historical results carry dates rather than conclusions about methods. Every calibration curve is a compilation of dated samples measured by particular laboratories, and its accuracy is limited by the dated material available at the time and by the agreement of the laboratories that measured it; when a new, denser body of tree-ring data arrives for a period that was thinly sampled before, the curve changes shape in that period and dates calibrated against the old shape move. The consequence for a long-running debate is not that somebody was wrong in the ordinary way but that the question had been settled by an artefact of the calibration, and reopening it is the correct response. The practical lesson for a reader is to ask when a calibration was published and what new data underpins it, and to prefer a statement of the form within a range of years, on a stated curve, over a single confident year.
questions.hint: Ask what the older curve was built from, and what a new body of data can change about it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The comparison that made a method credible
questions.learningObjective: explain why a method is tested on material whose answer is already known
questions.stem: A dating method is assessed by having several laboratories measure the same set of samples drawn from wood of known calendar age, and by seeing whether the laboratories agree. Which feature of that design is doing the work?

options.text: The samples are identical, so the spread between laboratories measures the samples rather than the laboratories
options.misconception: confuses which variable the spread measures

options.text: The samples are drawn from wood, so the test establishes that the method works on wood and on nothing else
options.misconception: reads a material-specific result as a general one

options.text: Several laboratories take part, so the design demonstrates that the method is cheap enough to be used widely
options.misconception: infers cost from the number of participants

options.text: The true ages are known, so each laboratory can be scored against an answer it could not have derived, and a method whose errors are large or inconsistent shows up as a spread rather than as an average

questions.explanation: The logic of the design is the logic of scoring against a known answer, and it is the same logic as any check on a measuring instrument, extended to the point where the instrument is a laboratory with several people and a method with several steps. Wood of known calendar age can be had because tree-ring sequences provide wood whose outermost ring is dated by a match to a series running to the present, so the true age of the material is known independently of the method being tested. Each laboratory's results can then be compared with it, and the comparison has two outputs: whether the error is small, and whether the laboratories agree with one another, which is the property that matters when the method is used by a laboratory the reader has never heard of. The last option is a non sequitur that is easy to check for, and the third is a genuine limitation of any such test rather than a defect in its design, since a method validated on one material has still to be shown on others.
questions.hint: Ask where the known ages come from, and what the spread between laboratories measures.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An offset between laboratories
questions.learningObjective: compute what a laboratory offset does to a derived date
questions.stem: In a large comparison, the same samples of known-age wood were sent to many laboratories. Some laboratories were consistently within ten years of the value the wood's calendar age implies, three showed offsets of ten to twenty years, and others showed larger and more variable offsets running to twenty or thirty years, varying from sample to sample. A study concludes that a single date should be reported with an uncertainty that includes the laboratory's own performance. Which conclusion about one reported date follows most directly?

options.text: A date produced by one laboratory carries an uncertainty of at least the size of that laboratory's observed offset, so a date quoted to the year overstates what the comparison supports
A date produced by one laboratory should be replaced by the average of all the laboratories, since an average removes the laboratory effect entirely
options.misconception: presumes an average that eliminates rather than averages a spread

options.text: A date is reliable if and only if the laboratory reports a tight uncertainty, since a stated precision measures the accuracy achieved
options.misconception: equates a stated precision with an accuracy established elsewhere

options.text: Only the laboratories that agreed should be allowed to date, since the others cannot be trusted to measure anything at all
options.misconception: proposes exclusion where a correction is the appropriate response

questions.explanation: The comparison's finding is a systematic difference between laboratories rather than random scatter, and a systematic difference of unknown sign is a source of error that no amount of care by the reader can remove. It follows that the uncertainty attached to a date has two parts: the uncertainty of the measurement itself, which the laboratory reports, and the uncertainty contributed by the laboratory's calibration and its performance, which only a comparison reveals and which is not in the report. Adding a laboratory component is the defensible response, and the third option is the trap, since a tight stated uncertainty measures the reproducibility of one instrument on one day and says nothing about the offset. The second is a common wish, and an average over laboratories is a real improvement where the offsets are small and unknown in sign, but it is not a cure where some laboratories vary from sample to sample, and it costs the reader the ability to see that the spread existed.
questions.hint: Ask what a stated uncertainty measures, and what a comparison of laboratories adds to it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why agreement between laboratories became the test
questions.learningObjective: explain a change in what counts as evidence in a measuring science
questions.stem: Explain why a date produced by one laboratory was eventually judged less convincing than the same date produced independently by several, and what that change did to the standing of published results.

answer.exemplar: The change is a change in what counts as evidence, and it follows from a recognition about what a measurement is. A single result is a report by one person, or by one instrument operated by one person, of one occasion, and everything that can go wrong can go wrong on that occasion: a contaminated preparation, a mislabelled vial, a calibration curve applied slightly wrongly, a transcription error, a sample that was not what the label said. None of these is detectable from inside the result, because a result carries no mark of its own origin. An independent replication is detectable in exactly the way a single result is not, because a preparation error or a contaminated vial does not recur in somebody else's laboratory while a systematic calibration offset does, and the difference between those two patterns is what makes the spread informative rather than merely discouraging. That is why the criterion became reproducibility rather than plausibility, and it is worth noticing what follows from the change. A published date ceases to be a statement about a sample and becomes a statement about a sample plus a laboratory, which is a more accurate description of what anyone actually had. It also means that the comparison itself becomes an instrument, and that a discipline's confidence in a period of its past is a function of how many laboratories have looked at that period. Two consequences follow that a historian should welcome. The first is that disagreement becomes informative rather than embarrassing, since a spread between laboratories is a measurement of the field's uncertainty, and a field with a large spread in one region of its chronology is telling you that the region is not yet settled. The second is that a single spectacular date is weaker evidence than a modest date replicated across laboratories, even when the spectacular date is more precise, because precision on its own does not carry information about the error that matters. The reappraisal of long-running debates when a calibration curve is revised is the same phenomenon at a larger scale, and the general rule is that a discipline's confidence in a period of its past is a function of how many independent observations of that period exist and how well they agree.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order in which a site's deposits become a chronology
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a deposit acquires a date
questions.stem: The steps by which an excavated deposit acquires a date that can be used in a history are set out below. Place them in the order in which they must happen.

options.text: Samples are selected from the deposit by a recorded rule that says which part of the context they represent
The excavation removes the deposit in recorded sections, so the order of the layers is preserved and can be read later
The sample is measured, and the measurement is converted into a range of calendar years with a stated uncertainty
The range is attached to the layer the sample came from, and the layer is attached to an event, so the deposit can be placed in a history

questions.explanation: The order runs from preserving the sequence to interpreting it, and every step after the first depends on the one before having been recorded rather than remembered. Digging in section comes first, because a deposit's value lies in its relationship to the layers above and below it, and that relationship exists only if the removal was recorded as it happened; a deposit lifted out in one piece has already lost the information that makes it datable in historical terms. Choosing samples by a stated rule comes second, since a date attaches to what was sampled and the choice of sample is therefore part of the argument about what the deposit dates. Measurement and conversion come third, and the conversion is where the uncertainty enters and must be stated. Attaching the range to a layer and a layer to an event is last, and it is the step most often done loosely, since a layer can contain several events and a date can be transferred from a material to an event only through an argument about the material's relation to the event.
questions.hint: Ask which step destroys information if it is not recorded, and which step introduces uncertainty.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A floor and the room above it
questions.learningObjective: explain what two floors in a building date
questions.stem: A building has an earlier floor, a layer of rubble, and a later floor laid over it, and each floor contains a dated deposit. Which statement about the two dates is best supported?

options.text: The two dates are the dates of the two builders, since each floor was laid by a different person on the day it was laid
options.misconception: confuses a deposit's date with a person's activity

options.text: The later date bounds when the first room was out of use, since the rubble had to be put there and the second floor laid before the room was reused
The two dates show that the building was repaired twice, since a gap between floors is a repair
options.misconception: infers a repair from a floor sequence

options.text: The earlier date is the more reliable, since the second floor was laid on rubble and therefore cannot be dated
options.misconception: supplies a physical impossibility for the later date

questions.explanation: A floor is a surface, and a surface is dated by what was on it, so two floors give two dates that are related in a particular way rather than merely repeated. The later floor cannot have been laid until the earlier room had been given up, filled and levelled, so the later date is a bound on the abandonment of the first room rather than a separate event, and the interval between the two dates is a period during which the building stood half ruined. That interval is often more informative than either date, since it is a measure of how long a structure was allowed to stand before it was rebuilt, and that is a fact about a community's resources and priorities rather than about its chronology. The fourth option is worth noticing because it gets the reasoning exactly backwards: a floor laid over rubble is more datable than one laid on soil, since the rubble gives a clear stratigraphic relationship between the two.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen between the two dates for the second floor to exist.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a monument records
questions.learningObjective: state what an inscribed stone does and does not attest
questions.stem: A ruler sets up a stone in a public place carrying a long text giving a date, the ruler's titles, an account of a campaign, and a list of the ruler's ancestors, and the practice is repeated by successors. Which statement about the evidence this provides is best supported?

options.text: The stones are a record of the population, since the ancestors named in them can be counted to give the size of a ruling house over time
options.misconception: reads a genealogy as a demographic count

options.text: The stones are a record of the economy, since a list of titles names the offices that a state required to function
options.misconception: reads an administrative list as an economic record

options.text: The stones are a record of the defeated, since an account of a campaign by its victors is the only surviving testimony of those conquered
options.misconception: treats a victor as the sole witness to a defeat

options.text: The stones are a record of what each reign asserted about itself, which is excellent evidence for what a court wanted known and for the sequence of reigns, and poor evidence for what happened

questions.explanation: The value of a monumental text and its limits come from the same fact, which is that it was made to be read by an audience with an interest in it. As a record of a sequence of reigns it is excellent, because a dated monument anchors a ruler to a calendar and a ruler anchors the monuments of other reigns to a sequence, and that is how most regional chronologies are assembled. As a record of events it is a statement by an interested party, and it is at its weakest exactly where it seems most detailed, since a king's account of a campaign is written to be set up in the city. The third option is a genuinely useful inference, since a list of offices does tell you something about what a state had to administer, but it is an inference from a purpose to a structure rather than a record of one or the other. The fourth is the standard error of treating victors' accounts as neutral on the grounds that somebody has to write it down, and the defeated leave traces of their own.
questions.hint: Ask who the text was written for, and what that does to each kind of claim it makes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A terminal date on a stone
questions.learningObjective: infer what a cessation of a record does and does not show
questions.stem: At a group of cities in a lowland region, the last dated monument in each case falls at a different date, the spread between the earliest and the latest is about a century, and occupation continues at several of the sites afterwards without monumental building. Which statement about the pattern is best supported?

options.text: The cities were destroyed at the dates their monuments show, since a ruler who stops cutting a date has stopped ruling
options.misconception: treats a record's end as an event's end

options.text: The spread of a century shows that a single event caused the change, since a single event cannot produce different dates at different sites
options.misconception: infers a common cause from a chronological spread

options.text: The cities ceased to record themselves in this way at different times and did not cease to exist, since a change in monumental practice and a change in population are different findings that need different evidence
The monuments show that the population declined, since monumental building requires a surplus and a surplus requires people
options.misconception: reads a change in building into a change in population

questions.explanation: The cessation of a record is a first-order datum and a second-order inference has to be built on it, and the two are very often conflated because the first is easy to measure and the second is what everybody wants. A ruler's last dated monument bounds the end of a practice, and a practice has causes that are not the same as the causes of a population's decline: a change of dynasty, a change of what a king was supposed to do, a shortage of stone, a change in where the court was, or simply a change in who could read. The case makes the point well because the two are separated here, since occupation continues at several of the sites after the last date, which is a direct demonstration that the record and the settlement came apart. The third option is the logic of a single event backwards, since one event affecting several sites at slightly different times is what a single event looks like, and the fourth reads a change in building directly into a change in people, which is exactly the inference the evidence cannot carry.
questions.hint: Ask what stopped, and what would have to be measured to show that anything else stopped too.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The direction a decline did not run
questions.learningObjective: use a spatial analysis to qualify a general claim
questions.stem: A study collects the last dated monument from each of about ninety sites in a lowland region, maps them, and tests the earlier proposal that abandonment ran in a single direction across the region, finding instead that the polities contracted around a small number of areas and that the abandonments in each area were spread over intervals of between a few decades and a century. Which finding is the more useful correction to the earlier proposal?

options.text: The contraction around a small number of areas, since it replaces a single directional sweep with a pattern of local contractions at different times, which is a different claim with different implications
The spread of the intervals within each area, since intervals of a century show that the process was too slow to be a collapse at all
options.misconception: treats a duration as a refutation of the word collapse

options.text: The size of the sample, since ninety sites is too few to support any regional claim about direction
options.misconception: dismisses a sample as too small without saying what would be large enough

options.text: The absence of a directional pattern, since a process with no direction cannot have a cause, since causes act in particular directions
options.misconception: denies that a cause can act without a spatial gradient

questions.explanation: The two findings do different work, and the one worth pressing is the first. A directional sweep and a set of local contractions are different models of the same process, with different implications for the question that matters, which is whether the region failed as a system or whether parts of it failed at different times and for local reasons while other parts held. The finding that abandonment is organised around a few areas and is not simultaneous within them is therefore the substantive result, while the range of intervals is a measure of the pace of the process, which is a different kind of information and does not by itself decide whether to use the word collapse. The fourth option is a logical error worth naming, because a cause need not act with a spatial gradient: a change in rainfall, a change in a trade route, or a political fragmentation produces different local chronologies without any of them pointing anywhere in particular.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two findings changes the model of the process, and which only measures its pace.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A cause whose evidence comes from where the effect was weakest
questions.learningObjective: assess a cause whose supporting evidence is poorly distributed
questions.stem: A region's cities decline, and the evidence for a drought comes chiefly from the northern part of the region, where the decline was later and less severe than in the southern part. Critics observe that the evidence for the cause is thickest where its effect is thinnest. Which statement about that criticism is best supported?

options.text: The criticism is mistaken, since a drought is regional and the absence of evidence in the south is only a gap in the record
options.misconception: dismands a distribution problem as a gap in the record

options.text: The criticism identifies a real weakness, since a cause evidenced in the place where it did least harm cannot easily account for the greater harm elsewhere, and the distribution of the cause and of its effect has to be explained
The criticism is mistaken, since the south is where the cities were largest and a large city generates more evidence of every kind
options.misconception: explains a pattern of evidence as a function of city size

options.text: The criticism is mistaken, since a cause and its effect are not required to be strongest in the same place
options.misconception: grants the point in terms that make the criticism irrelevant

questions.explanation: The criticism is the kind that should be pressed on any claim of this shape, because a cause is only an explanation if it explains the pattern of the effect and not merely the presence of it. If the drying is best evidenced in the north, where the cities held out longest, then the correlation between drying and decline in the north is weak, and a critic who says so is not being pedantic but pointing out that the case has been built where it was easiest to build. There are honest answers, and a study can make them: the southern record of drying may be poorer but still present, as a later analysis of the southern sediments argues; the northern cities may have had water storage, institutions or a different crop that carried them through; and a cause need not be uniform to be general. The point is that these are arguments to be made rather than a defect to be assumed away, and the fourth option is worth noticing because the claim it makes is true and irrelevant: a cause does not have to be strongest where the harm is greatest, but it does have to be shown to be capable of the harm that occurred.
questions.hint: Ask where the cause is evidenced and where the effect was greatest, and whether the two distributions match.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A region that recovered
questions.learningObjective: use a counter-case to bound a general claim
questions.stem: The cities of a lowland region decline, and a study of the region documents one city that after the general decline began shows a period of substantial new building, and a city to the north that grows larger and richer for a century afterwards. Which use of these two cases is best supported?

options.text: They disprove the general claim, since two counter-examples are sufficient to defeat a claim about the majority
options.misconception: treats counter-examples as a refutation

options.text: They confirm the general claim, since the exceptions show that the region's cities were of very unequal strength to begin with
options.misconception: reads exceptions as support for a generalisation

options.text: They show the decline was caused by a foreign invasion, since a region that was invaded and recovered must have repelled the invaders
options.misconception: infers a cause from the fact of recovery

options.text: They bound the general claim, since a process that stopped in one place and reversed in another cannot be described by a single verb applied to the whole region, and the differences between the places become the interesting question

questions.explanation: A counter-case is useful for bounding a claim and is not useful for killing one, which is the distinction this item turns on. A claim about a majority of the cities of a region is compatible with two exceptions, and the exceptions are not noise, because they are the places where the outcome differed and the difference is therefore evidence about the conditions on which the outcome depended. Once a study has documented them, the productive question changes from whether the decline happened to why it happened in one place and not in another, and the answer is usually to be found in water, land, institutions and position rather than in a single event. The second option is the standard mistake and it is worth naming precisely because a student is often told to look for counter-examples and then told that finding one refutes the claim; the second is a claim about a region, and a claim about a region is refuted by showing that the region as a whole did not decline, which two cities do not show.
questions.hint: Ask what a counter-case does to a claim about a majority, and what it tells you about the cases that differ.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An anchor site and the model built on it
questions.learningObjective: assess the structure of an argument that rests on a single site
questions.stem: For decades it was held that the first people in a continent carried a distinctive technology, and the model was built on a small number of sites of that technology. A site found far to the south, dated well before any of them, changed the model, and several further sites were then reported with the same implication, though each is disputed on the details of its dating or its integrity. Which statement about the model is best supported?

options.text: The model has been disproved, since one site dated earlier than the others is sufficient to establish that the first arrivals carried a different technology
options.misconception: treats one contested site as decisive

options.text: The model has been replaced, since the new sites agree with one another and a group of agreeing sites settles the question
options.misconception: treats agreement among sites as settling a question about people

options.text: The model rested on the earliest well-dated example of a technology rather than on the earliest arrival of people, and the distinction is the point at which a new site either overturns the model or only complicates it
The model is unaffected, since a site's date is a technical question and a model about people is not decided by a date
options.misconception: insists a technical and a historical question are wholly separate

questions.explanation: The first thing to establish about any such model is what it identifies with the beginning, and the commonest error is a slide from the earliest well-evidenced example to the earliest arrival. A technology with a recognisable form has a beginning in the record, but the beginning of a form is not the beginning of the people who made it, since a form can be adopted, can appear late among people who have been there for centuries, and can be imitated. A site that predates the earliest known examples of the form is therefore a serious complication, and a well-dated one is a refutation of the specific claim that the form marks the arrival. A disputed one is a complication that a reader should weigh by weighing its dating and its integrity, which is what the several new sites in this case require. And note the fourth option: the date of a site is not only a technical question, because a date determines whether a model about people has to change, and a model that ignores a relevant date has not been insulated from the technical question, it has simply not noticed it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the model claims the earliest example or the earliest arrival, and whether the new sites are secure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A flood that reorders a valley
questions.learningObjective: explain how a single event can rearrange the evidence of many
questions.stem: A river in flood scours one terrace and deposits silt on another, and an excavation of the two terraces shows a well-stratified sequence on one and a jumble of mixed occupation on the other. Which statement about the second terrace is best supported?

options.text: The jumble is the work of the flood, so the deposits on that terrace have lost the sequence a chronology depends on, and what survives there is usable for presence and date but not for order
The jumble shows that the occupation there was disorderly, since a mixed deposit is the signature of people living without rules
options.misconception: reads a depositional process as a social condition

options.text: The jumble shows the terrace was used as a rubbish dump, since mixed material is what accumulates where waste is thrown
options.misconception: assigns a purpose from a depositional signature

options.text: The jumble is unimportant, since a chronology is built from well-stratified deposits and the rest can be ignored
options.misconception: rules out a deposit rather than bounding its use

questions.explanation: A flood is a very efficient sorting machine, and its effect on a terrace is to remove the one property that archaeology depends on, which is the order of the deposits. On the scoured terrace the flood took everything and put it back; on the buried one it sealed the sequence under silt and preserved it, which is why the two terraces produce such different records of the same valley. What survives in a jumble is still worth having, since a sealed pot is a dated presence and a group of sealed pots is a dated horizon, but the relationship between two deposits in the jumble is gone and no amount of excavation will recover it. The fourth option states a real principle badly, because the useful discipline is bounding what a deposit can be used for rather than discarding it, and a presence without an order is exactly the kind of datum that dates a site without dating its sequence.
questions.hint: Ask what property of a deposit the flood removed, and what a deposit without it can still support.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A site that is now contested
questions.learningObjective: assess a challenge to a site's date while it is being disputed
questions.stem: A site found in the 1970s was reported as far older than anything then known on its continent, and it was quickly accepted as decisive against a prevailing model. A study published in 2026 argues that the site is much younger than reported, on the grounds that a stream has carried older organic material into deeper layers than the material that gave the original dates, and the excavators of the original work reject the new interpretation. Which statement about the pair of positions is soundest?

options.text: The dispute is about the calibration, since a date that is too old must have been calibrated against the wrong curve
options.misconception: locates the disagreement in a curve neither side is invoking

options.text: The dispute is about the sequence of deposition rather than about the measurement, since a chemical test cannot distinguish material that was buried in place from material that was carried in, and a replication can settle it
The new study has settled the matter, since a later study with modern methods supersedes an excavation of the 1970s
options.misconception: substitutes recency for evidence

options.text: The original date stands, since the excavators were the only people present when the site was found
options.misconception: grants priority of observation as if it settled interpretation

questions.explanation: The interesting thing about this case is the kind of error each side is diagnosing, and both are ordinary. A laboratory can only report the carbon in what it was given, and if a stream has moved old wood down into a layer containing younger material then a perfectly executed test returns a perfectly executed but wrong answer, and no amount of replication inside the laboratory will detect it. That is a fact about the site's formation rather than about the measurement, and it is the kind of thing a re-examination of the sediments can address, which is what the new study attempted. Meanwhile the original excavators' objection is a real one, since the re-interpretation depends on an account of how the layers were laid down and they are the people who watched it happen. The general lesson is that a date taken from a layer is a joint claim about the layer and the date, and a challenge that can be framed as a claim about the layer is a stronger challenge than one framed as a claim about the instrument.
questions.hint: Ask whether the disagreement is about the measurement or about what was measured, and which can be settled by looking again.
